newsitem.title: POLAND: POLISH PREMIER PLAYS DOWN RUSSIA SPY WARNING.
newsitem.headline: POLISH PREMIER PLAYS DOWN RUSSIA SPY WARNING.

text.p: Poland's prime minister on Monday played down warnings by security chief Zbigniew Siemiatkowski that Russian intelligence was preparing underhand efforts to discredit Poland and block its NATO and European Union entry.
Asked to comment on Siemiatkowski's remarks, Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz told a news conference countries opposed to Poland's NATO bid might try various ways to halt it.
But Cimoszewicz, ultimately in charge of the security service, added: "I would be talking more in terms of some potential risk than any very important danger existing now."

Siemiatkowski, in an interview with Saturday's Rzeczpospolita daily just before he began a visit to his security counterparts in Germany, alleged Russian agents were cultivating links with government and opposition politicians.

Rzeczpospolita quoted Siemiatkowski as saying he expected Russian's services to stage provocations aimed at discrediting the drive by Poland, which escaped Moscow's domination with the fall of communism in 1989, to join European structures.
"They will show that countries aspiring to NATO have unreliable elites -- corrupt on the one side and loyal to their former bosses on the other," he said.
The comments by Siemiatkowski, minister in charge of the security service, displeased Foreign Minister Dariusz Rosati.

"Taking this kind of anxiety to the media and speaking of this in the framework of public debate may not be the best idea," Rosati said, although he conceded that it was the job of the security services to be alert and anything was possible.

Rosati told public radio Poland was on track to get an invitation to begin talks on joining NATO at the pact's July summit in Madrid. Poland expects, along with at least the Czech Republic and Hungary, to enter the Western pact in 1999.

Russian politicians have denounced NATO's planned inclusion of neighbouring Poland as a threat to its security, although Polish analysts say Moscow is chiefly afraid of losing its former sphere of influence over eastern central Europe.
Recently some Russian commentators have also expressed worries over Polish entry into the European Union, another top goal of the country of nearly 40 million people.
Rosati said there had recently been greater anti-NATO activity in formerly pacifist or leftist circles in the West.
"But I don't think these are forces influential enough to in any way brake or derail the process. I am a limited optimist and think NATO expansion will go ahead as planned," he said.

Siemiatkowski, like Cimoszewicz, is a member of the dominant ex-communists in Poland's ruling coalition -- a party widely seen as more vulnerable to Russian influence than opposition groups descended from the Solidarity movement.
Early last year the party's previous prime minister, Jozef Oleksy was forced to quit following security service allegations he had knowingly informed for Moscow agents.

Oleksy strongly denied the allegations, although admitting an unwise acquaintance with Russian diplomat Vladimir Alganov who later proved to be an intelligence officer, and prosecutors dropped the case saying the evidence was flawed and inadequate.
Polish newspapers were full of speculation about why Siemiatkowski had chosen to make public his apprehensions now.
But Adam Michnik, editor of the Gazeta Wyborcza daily drew a simple moral for Poland's political elite:
"Be on your guard, gentlemen. Learn from the sad story of Alganov's close contacts with Jozef Oleksy."
